theory.title: Theory and what to observe
theory.rle: RLE replaces runs of equal bytes with (count, value); it gains little on ordinary audio.
theory.huffman: Canonical Huffman gives frequent symbols short codes and derives code lengths from the histogram; nothing is lost.
theory.delta: The first-order predictor codes differences between adjacent samples; the smaller range makes Huffman more compact.
theory.companding: μ-law and A-law (G.711) compress amplitude logarithmically; 8 bits sound acceptable but are not bit-exact.
theory.mdct: A windowed MDCT with TDAC turns the signal into coefficients; uniform quantization under a bit budget produces playback-friendly error.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.lossless: RLE, Huffman and delta+Huffman must show “bit-exact ✓”; μ-law, A-law and MDCT must not.
observe.entropy: Compare the lossless size with entropy; the coder approaches the theoretical bound.
observe.bitrate: In MDCT, sweep the bitrate and watch SNR/PSNR against bitrate.
observe.sparsity: MDCT coefficient sparsity shows how much quantization zeroes out.

observe.magnitude: Editing magnitude keeps phase; zeroing magnitude zeros Re and Im together.
observe.phase: Editing phase keeps magnitude; zeroing phase sets it to zero.
observe.hermitian: With Hermitian symmetry on, the output stays real; turning it off shows why the symmetry is needed.
observe.gibbs: Zeroing a whole band produces Gibbs ringing in the output; sharp truncation causes it.

metrics.theoryNote: The theoretical 6.02·N + 1.76 dB assumes a full-scale sine and no dither.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.aliasing: Turn the anti-alias filter off and lower the target rate: a tone above the new Nyquist appears at a different frequency.
observe.dither: At low bit depth, dither replaces correlated quantization distortion with a steady noise floor.
observe.snr: Each extra bit adds about 6 dB of SNR; compare the measured value with the theoretical line.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.truncate: A shorter truncation widens the main lobe and raises the bin width Δf = fs / N.
observe.zeroPad: Zero-padding adds no new information: it samples the same spectrum more densely, so the main-lobe width stays the same.
observe.tradeoff: A signal that is narrow in time is wide in frequency (time–bandwidth uncertainty).
observe.scale: Time scaling moves the spectrum inversely: x(at) has spectrum |a|⁻¹ X(f/a).
observe.periodic: Periodic extension produces spectral lines at multiples of 1/T.
observe.scaleNote: Time scaling deliberately has no anti-alias filter. For the filtered comparison, use the sampling lab (F03).
observe.units: Energy and average power are amplitude-squared values; for normalized audio in [−1, 1] the unit is full-scale².

timing.title: FFT vs direct convolution timing
timing.note: Measured on a 4096-sample excerpt with a short impulse response, not on the whole file.

steps.title: Convolution step by step
steps.note: Each partial is the signal scaled by one IR tap and shifted by that tap's index. Their sum is the direct convolution.

reverse.title: Reverse (time reversal)
reverse.note: Reverse flips the signal in time. It is a separate operation from reverb: no impulse response and no wet/dry mix are involved.
reverse.empty: Select at least two samples to compare spectra.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.reverse: Time reversal keeps the magnitude spectrum; the phase is conjugated plus a linear phase term. It is not reverb.
observe.reverb: Reverb convolves the signal with an impulse response; a longer IR adds a longer tail.
observe.tail: The output keeps the full convolution tail: pre-delay + source length + IR length − 1 samples.
observe.direct: Direct convolution is easy to read but grows with source length × IR length; the FFT path is faster for long inputs.
observe.ir: Changing the IR seed changes the noise detail, not the RT60 decay envelope or the overall energy.

theory.title: Definitions and what to observe
theory.energy: SNR compares signal energy with error energy; MSE averages the squared sample error and is sensitive to outliers.
theory.segmental: Segmental SNR averages per-frame SNR over 20 ms active frames, so a bad short passage is not hidden by a good average.
theory.psnr: PSNR = 10·log10(peak² / MSE) with peak = 1.0 for full-scale float audio.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.lossless: A lossless codec still differs from the float original by 16-bit PCM quantization error; SNR is finite and PSNR is large.
observe.lossy: Lower lossy bitrates raise MSE and lower SNR/PSNR; listen to the same result for the perceptual difference.
observe.bitrate: Compare several codec settings and relate the metric change to the bitrate shown in the compression lab.

caption.approximation: AI-generated approximation: compare it with the original before drawing conclusions.

concept.heading: How the model suppresses noise
concept.body: The model estimates a time-frequency mask from noisy speech and multiplies it with the complex spectrum. Unlike a fixed high-pass filter, the suppression follows speech and noise patterns learned from data.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Compare the enhanced speech with the noisy demo and listen for the same events.

bullets.noise: Noise between words should drop more than speech onsets.
bullets.artifacts: Listen for musical noise or smeared consonants; over-suppression removes detail.
bullets.shape: The waveform and spectrogram should keep the same duration and sample rate.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: Denoising can improve listening but hurt a downstream recognizer. AI output is an approximation, not a recovered clean recording.

bullets.speechLoss: A high mask can delete weak speech sounds as well as noise.
bullets.notRecovered: Artifacts remain; do not present the result as the original clean source.

concept.heading: Extension versus interpolation
concept.body: Sinc interpolation can only fill between existing samples, while a learned model predicts plausible content above the old Nyquist frequency from the low band.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Compare the learned result with the sinc baseline on the same speech clip.

bullets.spectrum: LavaSR should extend energy above the cutoff; interpolation leaves a hard band edge.
bullets.brightness: Listen for added brightness against a dull, band-limited copy.
bullets.plausibility: Decide whether new high-frequency detail sounds plausible or artificial.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: The model cannot restore information that was never recorded; it invents plausible detail. AI output is an approximation.

bullets.invented: Treat high-band content as generated, not recovered.
bullets.rates: Different sample rates must be mapped back explicitly before listening or measuring.

concept.heading: Separating by time-frequency masks
concept.body: A separator estimates one mask or waveform per stem in the time-frequency domain, then reconstructs each source. The stems add back to an approximation of the mix, not to the exact original tracks.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Solo each stem and then compare their sum with the mix.

bullets.solo: Vocals should dominate the vocal stem and drums the drum stem.
bullets.bleed: Listen for bleed and hollow artifacts where another source was removed.
bullets.sum: The summed stems should resemble the original mix, with some error.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: Separation is not unmixing the original studio tracks; overlap and reverb cause errors. AI output is an approximation.

bullets.notTracks: Do not claim access to the master tracks; the output is estimated.
bullets.excerpt: CPU runs use a short excerpt, so a full-file result is not implied.

concept.heading: Acoustic model, language model, and WER
concept.body: An acoustic model maps frames to text tokens and a language model resolves ambiguous sounds. WER counts substitutions, deletions, and insertions over the reference word count.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Keep the reference transcript fixed while you change the codec setting.

bullets.reference: Compare the transcript with the bundled reference after each codec.
bullets.bitrate: Lower bitrates usually raise WER, but a denoiser can also hurt recognition.
bullets.normalization: The checker normalizes case, punctuation, and whitespace before counting.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: The transcript is an AI approximation, not a guaranteed caption. WER requires an aligned reference and honest normalization.

bullets.alignment: Do not compare raw strings without the documented normalization.
bullets.persian: Tiny models are weak for Persian; use the English speech demo for this experiment.

concept.heading: Residual vector quantization
concept.body: A neural codec encodes the signal as indices into learned codebooks. Residual vector quantization refines the waveform in stages; more stages or larger codebooks raise the bitrate and usually lower distortion.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Move across bitrates and compare decoded audio with the original.

bullets.bitrates: Compare at least low, medium, and high bitrate settings.
bullets.rateDistortion: Watch the neural point against the traditional codec points.
bullets.artifacts: At very low rates the codec keeps structure but loses detail.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: A neural codec is not bit-exact and its delay must be aligned before metrics. Decoded audio is an AI approximation.

bullets.alignment: Align codec delay before computing SNR or PSNR.
bullets.stages: Reported bitrate includes every quantizer stage; do not compare only one.

error.invalid: The cutoff must lie inside (0, Nyquist). Check the cutoff, band edges, order, taps, and ripple.
error.designFailed: Filter design failed. Check the parameters and try again.
error.playback: The filtered result does not fit the playback caps.
error.applyFailed: Applying the filter failed. Try a shorter excerpt.

filters.delayNote: A linear-phase FIR reports and compensates its group delay for preview alignment. The causal IIR response is not trimmed.
filters.unstableWarning: This design is unstable (a pole lies outside the unit circle); apply is disabled.

plots.empty: Not enough finite data to draw this plot.

poleZero.title: Pole-zero plane
poleZero.aria: Pole-zero plot with the unit circle
poleZero.omitted: Roots are omitted for FIR designs above 33 taps.

transfer.heading: Transfer function
transfer.body: A linear time-invariant filter is described by a rational transfer function in z. The roots of the numerator are zeros and the roots of the denominator are poles.

fir.heading: FIR window method
fir.body: Sample the ideal response and truncate it with a window. A wider window narrows the transition band; a smoother window lowers the side lobes.

butterworth.heading: Butterworth response
butterworth.body: Butterworth is maximally flat in the passband and steepens as the order rises.

chebyshev.heading: Chebyshev type I response
chebyshev.body: Chebyshev type I accepts small passband ripple to get a sharper transition at the same order.

groupDelay.heading: Group delay
groupDelay.body: Group delay is the derivative of phase with frequency; it describes the delay of a narrow-band envelope, not the phase delay of each sinusoid.

poles.heading: Poles and stability
poles.body: Inside the unit circle is stable, outside is unstable, and on the circle is marginal. A pole closer to the circle produces a sharper resonance and slower decay.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Change one control at a time and compare these four effects.

bullets.cutoff: Cutoff sets the edge; the transition width depends on the order or the FIR tap count and window.
bullets.order: Higher order or a longer FIR gives a steeper transition but more ringing near the edge.
bullets.linearPhase: A symmetric FIR has linear phase; the price is a delay of about (taps − 1) / 2 samples.
bullets.poles: Poles near the unit circle produce a visible resonance and a longer impulse response.

pitfalls.heading: Common pitfalls
pitfalls.body: These three mistakes cause most confusion.

bullets.nyquist: A cutoff at or above Nyquist is invalid; the design is rejected.
bullets.unstable: An IIR design with a pole outside the unit circle is unstable and must not be applied.
bullets.delay: Phase delay and group delay are not the same; check the group-delay plot, not only the phase plot.

experiments.title: Guided experiments
experiments.intro: Each card is a short lab sheet. Open the linked lab, change one control at a time, and compare what you hear and see with the expected observation.

filters.title: Filter design: cutoff, order, and group delay
filters.goal: See how cutoff and order change the transition band, ringing, and group delay.

taps.instruction: Load the chirp demo and design an FIR low-pass with 101 taps at 4 kHz using a Hamming window.
taps.observation: With 101 taps the transition is wide and the magnitude rolls off around 4 kHz.

order.instruction: Switch to Butterworth with order 8 and keep the same cutoff.
order.observation: A higher order narrows the transition but adds ringing near the edge.

ripple.instruction: Switch to Chebyshev type I with order 8 and 0.5 dB ripple.
ripple.observation: Passband ripple appears, and the group delay peaks near the cutoff.

groupDelay.instruction: Return to FIR and read the group-delay and impulse-response plots.
groupDelay.observation: The symmetric FIR has a flat group delay away from the transition.

superres.title: Sampling and super-resolution: 8 kHz to full band
superres.goal: Separate a sample-rate change from true bandwidth extension on speech.

load.instruction: Load the clean speech demo in the super-resolution tab.
load.observation: The original spectrum fills the full band of the source rate.

sinc.instruction: Band-limit to 8 kHz and choose the sinc path.
sinc.observation: Sinc restores the sample rate but leaves a hard edge at 4 kHz; it creates no new high-band energy.

lavasr.instruction: Switch the restore path to LavaSR and compare the spectrum above 4 kHz.
lavasr.observation: LavaSR adds energy above 4 kHz; judge whether the detail is plausible or artificial.

asrCodec.title: Compression and recognition
asrCodec.goal: Connect codec bitrate with listening quality and see how a recognizer behaves on the original speech.

low.instruction: Load the speech demo and encode MDCT at 32 kbps.
low.observation: At 32 kbps the envelope survives but fine detail smears.

mid.instruction: Encode the same excerpt at 128 kbps.
mid.observation: Artifacts weaken and the waveform and spectrogram move closer to the original.

high.observation: For speech the result is close to transparent.

asr.instruction: Run ASR on the original speech and note its baseline WER.
asr.observation: ASR always reads the original source in this lab, so WER does not change with the codec setting; use listening and the spectrogram for the codec comparison.
